claims.text: When driving a car, given a proposed sequence of steering and pedal actions over several seconds, drivers can accurately predict the car's trajectory over that same period.
claims.quote: given a proposed sequence of actions on the steering wheel and pedals over the next several seconds, drivers can accurately predict the trajectory of their car over the same period

claims.text: Trajectory details over longer driving periods are harder to predict because they depend on unpredictable external events like other cars, traffic lights, and pedestrians.
claims.quote: The details of the trajectory over longer periods are harder to predict because they may depend on other cars, traffic lights, pedestrians, and other external events that are somewhat unpredictable

claims.text: Drivers can make accurate higher-level predictions about arrival times even when detailed trajectories are unpredictable.
claims.quote: the car will probably arrive at its destination within a predictable time frame

claims.text: Discrete latent variables can represent multiple alternative routes in hierarchical prediction.
claims.quote: A discrete latent variable may be used to represent multiple alternative routes

claims.text: Hierarchical world state prediction with multiple levels can use convolutional and other modules with temporal pooling between levels.
claims.quote: One can envision architectures of this type with many levels, possibly using convolutional and other modules, and using temporal pooling between levels to coarse-grain the representation and perform longer-term predictions

claims.text: The ability to represent world state sequences at several levels of abstraction is essential to intelligent behavior.
claims.quote: the ability to represent sequences of world states at several levels of abstraction is essential to intelligent behavior

claims.text: Complex tasks can be decomposed into hierarchically structured subtasks at different levels of detail, instantiated when local conditions permit.
claims.quote: With multi-level representations of world states and actions, a complex task can be decomposed into successively more detailed sub-tasks, instantiated into actions sequences when informed by local conditions

claims.text: Hierarchical planning architectures can learn intermediate action representations rather than requiring them to be predefined.
claims.quote: if one abides by the deep learning philosophy, those intermediate representations of action plans should also be learned

claims.text: In hierarchical Mode-2 planning, high-level actions are actually targets for lower-level predicted states, functioning as conditions that lower-level states must satisfy.
claims.quote: These high-level "actions" are not real actions but targets for the lower level predicted states. One can think of them as conditions that the lower-level state must satisfy in order for the high-level predictions to be accurate

claims.text: Cost modules measure the extent to which a lower-level state satisfies a high-level condition to define subgoals.
claims.quote: cost modules C(s[2]) and C(s[4]) take a lower-level state s[2] and a high-level condition a2[2] and measure to what extent the state satisfies the condition

claims.text: Top-down greedy hierarchical planning can be improved by jointly optimizing action sequences across all layers.
claims.quote: one may advantageously iterate the optimization so that high level and low-level action sequences are optimized jointly

claims.text: The concept that an action is a condition to be satisfied by the level below originates from classical control theory.
claims.quote: The idea that an action is merely a condition to be satisfied by the level below is actually an old one in control theory

claims.text: A proportional servomechanism from classical control theory can be understood as receiving a target state with quadratic cost measuring distance to that target.
claims.quote: a classical proportional servomechanism can be seen as being given a target state. A quadratic cost measures the squared distance between the target and the current state

claims.text: Real-world uncertainty can arise from the world being intrinsically stochastic (aleatoric uncertainty type 1).
claims.quote: the world is intrinsically stochastic (aleatoric uncertainty, type 1)

claims.text: Uncertainty can result from deterministic but chaotic worlds that are difficult to predict without infinitely precise perception (aleatoric uncertainty type 2).
claims.quote: the world is deterministic but chaotic, hence difficult to predict without infinitely precise perception (aleatoric uncertainty, type 2)

claims.text: Partial observability of a deterministic world creates aleatoric uncertainty (type 3).
claims.quote: the world is deterministic but partially observable (aleatoric uncertainty type 3)

claims.text: Epistemic uncertainty type 1 occurs when sensors provide only partial information about fully observable world states.
claims.quote: the world is fully observable, but the sensors only give partial information about the world state (epistemic uncertainty, type 1)

claims.text: Epistemic uncertainty type 2 occurs when the perception module's extracted representation lacks information necessary for accurate prediction.
claims.quote: the representation of the world state extracted by the perception module does not contain the full information necessary for accurate prediction (epistemic uncertainty, type 2)

claims.text: Epistemic uncertainty type 3 results from inaccurate world models due to limited representational power (bounded rationality).
claims.quote: the world model is inaccurate due to limitations of its representational power (bounded rationality or epistemic uncertainty, type 3)

claims.text: Latent variables in predictors can represent prediction information that cannot be derived from prior observations.
claims.quote: Uncertainty about predictions can be handled by predictors with latent variables. The latent variables contain information about the prediction that cannot be derived from the prior observation

claims.text: Latent variables must be regularized to prevent energy collapse and force the system to predict without their help.
claims.quote: The latent variables must be regularized to prevent an energy collapse and to force the system to predict as much as possible without the help of it

claims.text: At planning time, latent variables are sampled from distributions created by applying Gibbs distributions to regularizers, producing different predictions.
claims.quote: At planning time, latent variables are sampled from distributions obtained by applying a Gibbs distribution to the regularizers. Each sample leads to a different prediction

claims.text: Regularizer parameters can be functions of previous states and retrieved memories to produce consistent latent sequences.
claims.quote: the parameters of the regularizer can be functions of previous states and retrieved memories

claims.text: The number of generated state trajectories grows exponentially when each latent variable has k discrete values and prediction progresses t time steps (k^t trajectories).
claims.quote: If each latent variable has k possible discrete values, the number of possible trajectories will grow as k^t, where t is the number of time steps

claims.text: Directed search and pruning strategies are necessary to manage exponential growth in predicted trajectories.
claims.quote: Directed search and pruning strategies must be employed

claims.text: With multiple predicted trajectories, optimal action sequences can minimize average cost or combinations of average and variance to minimize risk.
claims.quote: optimal action sequences can be computed that minimize the average cost, or a combination of average and variance of the cost so as to minimize risk

candidates.title: Hierarchical world state prediction
candidates.why: Multi-level architecture (JEPA-1, JEPA-2) using temporal pooling to represent world states at different abstractions for short and long-term prediction.

candidates.title: Multi-scale representation
candidates.why: Core mechanism for representing world states and actions at multiple levels of abstraction to enable hierarchical decomposition of complex tasks.

candidates.title: Hierarchical planning (Mode-2 reasoning)
candidates.why: Architecture and approach for decomposing complex tasks into hierarchically structured subtasks using learned intermediate action representations.

candidates.title: JEPA (Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture)
candidates.why: Specific architecture mentioned for performing hierarchical predictions; appears as JEPA-1, JEPA-2 in Figure 15 and extended in Figures 16-17.

candidates.title: Action as condition satisfaction
candidates.why: Conceptual framework where high-level actions are viewed as conditions/targets for lower-level states to satisfy, with historical roots in control theory.

candidates.title: Cost modules
candidates.why: Components that measure the extent to which lower-level states satisfy high-level conditions, defining subgoals in hierarchical planning.

candidates.title: Aleatoric uncertainty
candidates.why: Classification of uncertainty types (1-3) due to stochasticity, chaos, or partial observability of the world rather than model limitations.

candidates.title: Epistemic uncertainty
candidates.why: Classification of uncertainty types (1-3) due to incomplete sensors, insufficient representation, or bounded rationality of world models.

candidates.title: Latent variable regularization
candidates.why: Mechanism for preventing energy collapse in predictors with latent variables and forcing prediction without relying on latent information.

candidates.title: Gibbs distribution for latent sampling
candidates.why: Technique for sampling latent variables during planning from distributions derived from regularizers.

candidates.title: Proportional servomechanism
candidates.why: Historical control theory example showing action as condition satisfaction, using quadratic cost to measure distance to target state.

candidates.title: Exponential trajectory growth in planning
candidates.why: Problem of k^t trajectory explosion when planning with k-valued latent variables across t timesteps, requiring pruning strategies.

candidates.title: Risk-minimizing action sequences
candidates.why: Planning approach that minimizes combinations of average cost and variance across multiple predicted trajectories.
